title: Polynomial-time planted-clique detection below the square-root scale
open: Can a randomized polynomial-time algorithm reliably tell an Erdős–Rényi graph \(G(n,1/2)\) apart from one containing a planted clique of size \(\lfloor n^{1/3}\rfloor\)? Formally, determine whether such an algorithm exists whose error probability tends to zero in this detection task.
status: This is a longstanding average-case complexity problem. Exhaustive search succeeds well below the regime reached by standard polynomial-time methods, and planted-clique assumptions support numerous conditional statistical lower bounds (e.g., Berthet and Rigollet, 2013; Brennan, Bresler, and Huleihel, 2018).
solved_when: A randomized polynomial-time algorithm is exhibited that distinguishes \(G(n,1/2)\) from the same model with a planted clique of size \(\lfloor n^{1/3}\rfloor\) with error tending to zero — or it is shown that no such algorithm exists.
why: A resolution would change computational feasibility claims across high-dimensional statistics, since planted-clique hardness underlies many conditional lower bounds in that area.
key_works: Berthet and Rigollet, 2013, “Complexity Theoretic Lower Bounds for Sparse Principal Component Detection,” PMLR 30; Brennan, Bresler, and Huleihel, 2018, “Reducibility and Computational Lower Bounds for Problems with Planted Sparse Structure,” arXiv:1806.07508.

title: Complete computational minimax frontier for sparse PCA
open: What is the best estimation risk achievable in polynomial time for a sparse leading eigenvector, as a function of sample size, ambient dimension, sparsity, and signal strength? A complete answer should cover the transition regimes, not just well-separated asymptotic cases.
status: Information-theoretic rates, efficient algorithms, and conditional hardness results cover substantial regions of the parameter space, but a single sharp computational risk characterization, including boundary behavior and constants, remains open. Key works include Berthet and Rigollet (2013), "Complexity Theoretic Lower Bounds for Sparse Principal Component Detection," and Brennan, Bresler, and Huleihel (2018), "Reducibility and Computational Lower Bounds for Problems with Planted Sparse Structure" (arXiv:1806.07508).
solved_when: A single sharp characterization of the polynomial-time minimax risk for sparse PCA is obtained across sample size, ambient dimension, sparsity, and signal strength, including boundary behavior and constants in the transition regimes.
why: It would identify when additional data can substitute for unavailable computation, separating statistical and computational resources in a concrete estimation problem.
key_works: Berthet and Rigollet, 2013, “Complexity Theoretic Lower Bounds for Sparse Principal Component Detection”; Brennan, Bresler, and Huleihel, 2018, “Reducibility and Computational Lower Bounds for Problems with Planted Sparse Structure,” arXiv:1806.07508.

title: Tensor PCA below known efficient thresholds
open: For a rank-one order-three tensor in Gaussian noise, how weak can the signal be while weak recovery still succeeds in polynomial time? More formally, determine the smallest signal-to-noise scale permitting polynomial-time weak recovery, and whether the resulting information–computation gap is intrinsic rather than an artifact of current algorithms.
status: The gap has been studied since at least 2014. Information-theoretic recovery and available algorithmic guarantees operate at different signal scales; computational conclusions depend on the algorithm class or hardness hypothesis. Related lines include statistical-physics analyses of glassy inference landscapes and low-degree polynomial lower bounds in computer science. Key work: Montanari and Richard, 2014, "A statistical model for tensor PCA," arXiv:1411.1076.
solved_when: The minimal signal scale for polynomial-time weak recovery of the rank-one order-three spiked tensor in Gaussian noise is determined, together with a resolution of whether the information–computation gap is intrinsic.
why: It would clarify the limits of higher-order latent-variable estimation, delimiting what is efficiently estimable when the inference landscape is glassy.
key_works: Montanari and Richard, 2014, “A statistical model for tensor PCA,” arXiv:1411.1076.

title: Submatrix detection with uncertain heterogeneous noise
open: When can an elevated-mean rectangle hidden in noisy data be detected, if the noise variances differ across entries and must themselves be estimated from limited auxiliary measurements? The goal is to derive matching statistical and computational detection boundaries for this unknown submatrix under heterogeneous, estimated variances.
status: The problem extends the established homogeneous submatrix model, whose computational barriers were characterized by Ma and Wu, 2015, "Computational barriers in minimax submatrix detection," arXiv:1309.5914, DOI:10.1214/14-AOS1300. Classical computational barriers do not by themselves characterize the interaction between variance-estimation error, rectangular sparsity, and signal strength. Related settings include planted dense-subgraph detection in computer science and detection under unknown noise fields in signal processing.
solved_when: Matching statistical and computational detection boundaries are derived, jointly characterizing how variance-estimation error, rectangular sparsity, and signal strength interact in the heterogeneous-noise submatrix detection model.
why: It would extend biclustering guarantees to unevenly measured biological and industrial data, where noise levels genuinely vary across measurements.
key_works: Ma and Wu, 2015, “Computational barriers in minimax submatrix detection,” arXiv:1309.5914, DOI:10.1214/14-AOS1300.

title: Universality for correlated non-Gaussian designs
open: When do the precise high-dimensional risk formulas of random-design regression remain valid once the design entries are both correlated and non-Gaussian? That is, find verifiable dependence conditions under which such formulas stay universal in that generality.
status: Universality is established for important independent-entry settings, while arbitrary isotropic designs admit counterexamples; the open problem is a useful intermediate class with sharp assumptions. See Han and Shen, 2023, "Universality of regularized regression estimators in high dimensions," arXiv:2206.07936, DOI:10.1214/23-AOS2309.
solved_when: A class of correlated, non-Gaussian designs is identified, with sharp and checkable dependence assumptions, for which the precise high-dimensional risk formulas are proven universal — going beyond the independent-entry settings while excluding the known counterexamples for arbitrary isotropic designs.
why: It would justify using Gaussian-derived predictions for realistic structured data, where independent-entry theory currently does not apply.
key_works: Han and Shen, 2023, “Universality of regularized regression estimators in high dimensions,” arXiv:2206.07936, DOI:10.1214/23-AOS2309.

title: Confidence sets through eigenvalue collisions
open: Can we construct honest confidence sets for spectral structure that adapt automatically between identifiable individual eigenvectors and only-identifiable invariant subspaces as the population eigengaps shrink at unknown rates?
status: Spectral-projector normal approximations provide a substantial baseline. Uniform inference across merging eigenvalues requires handling a changing identifiable parameter. A key reference is Koltchinskii and Lounici, 2017, “Normal approximation and concentration of spectral projectors of sample covariance,” arXiv:1504.07333, DOI:10.1214/16-AOS1437.
solved_when: A procedure exists that delivers honest coverage, remaining valid uniformly across merging eigenvalues where the identifiable parameter itself changes from eigenvectors to invariant subspaces, without knowledge of the eigengap shrinkage rate.
why: It prevents falsely precise principal-component interpretations near degeneracy.
key_works: Koltchinskii and Lounici, 2017, “Normal approximation and concentration of spectral projectors of sample covariance,” arXiv:1504.07333, DOI:10.1214/16-AOS1437.

title: Logistic-regression inference near the separation transition
open: When does high-dimensional logistic regression stop supporting reliable inference? Derive finite-size scaling laws and uniformly valid inference as the model approaches the boundary between existence and nonexistence of the maximum-likelihood estimator.
status: Modern proportional-asymptotic theory describes major departures from classical likelihood theory; the critical window and practical uncertainty statements across it remain a sharper target (Sur and Candès, 2019, “A modern maximum-likelihood theory for high-dimensional logistic regression,” arXiv:1803.06964, DOI:10.1073/pnas.1810420116).
solved_when: Finite-size scaling laws near the separation transition are derived, and inference procedures remain uniformly valid across the critical window between MLE existence and nonexistence.
why: It would identify when familiar coefficient estimates become fundamentally unstable.
key_works: Sur and Candès, 2019, “A modern maximum-likelihood theory for high-dimensional logistic regression,” arXiv:1803.06964, DOI:10.1073/pnas.1810420116.

title: Standard-assumption hardness for bounded-moment robust means
open: Are there computational lower bounds, under broadly accepted assumptions, that separate the information-theoretic robust mean rates achievable with bounded fourth or higher directional moments from what polynomial-time algorithms can achieve? A formal answer would exhibit a standard hardness assumption under which no efficient algorithm matches the optimal statistical rate.
status: Hardness results and algorithms depend strongly on whether moment conditions are merely true or efficiently certifiable, and this distinction remains central in the 2025 open-problem discussion (UW CSE 599K, 2025, “Lecture 18”; Hopkins and Li, 2019, “How hard is robust mean estimation?” arXiv:1903.07870).
solved_when: A computational lower bound is established under broadly accepted assumptions, showing a gap between the information-theoretic robust mean rate for bounded fourth (or higher) directional moments and the polynomial-time achievable rate.
why: A solution would explain whether weaker modeling assumptions necessarily cost computational efficiency, i.e., whether robustness under mere bounded-moment conditions forces a statistical–computational tradeoff.
key_works: Hopkins and Li, 2019, “How hard is robust mean estimation?” arXiv:1903.07870; UW CSE 599K, 2025, “Lecture 18.”

title: The sparse robust-mean sample gap
open: Can we match the information-theoretically minimal number of samples for estimating a sparse mean under adversarial contamination with a polynomial-time algorithm, or is there a fundamental computational barrier forcing a gap?
status: Efficient methods can require substantially worse sparsity dependence than unrestricted estimators; ordinary sparse estimation and ordinary robust estimation do not settle their combination. Related threads include sparse PCA hardness in computer science and efficient sparse private estimation in privacy, as in Georgiev and Hopkins, 2022, “Privacy Induces Robustness: Information-Computation Gaps and Sparse Mean Estimation,” arXiv:2211.00724, and Hopkins and Li, 2019, “How hard is robust mean estimation?”
solved_when: Either a polynomial-time estimator achieves the information-theoretic sample complexity for sparse mean estimation under adversarial contamination (matching sparsity dependence of unrestricted estimators), or a proof establishes a sharp separation between efficient and information-theoretic sample requirements.
why: It would support reliable feature discovery in contaminated high-dimensional data.
key_works: Georgiev and Hopkins, 2022, “Privacy Induces Robustness: Information-Computation Gaps and Sparse Mean Estimation,” arXiv:2211.00724; Hopkins and Li, 2019, “How hard is robust mean estimation?”

title: Simultaneous graph inference under cellwise contamination
open: When individual cells of a data table — rather than whole rows — are corrupted, with contamination rates that differ across coordinates, can we still recover the dependence structure? Construct simultaneous confidence statements for a sparse precision matrix in this cellwise contamination setting.
status: Robust precision-matrix estimation under cellwise contamination has a 2015 baseline (Loh and Tan, 2015, "High-dimensional robust precision matrix estimation: Cellwise corruption under ε-contamination," arXiv:1509.07229). Selection-valid edge inference and sharp uncertainty under heterogeneous contamination remain stronger targets.
solved_when: A method is given that yields simultaneous confidence statements for the entries of a sparse precision matrix under cellwise contamination with heterogeneous (coordinate-varying) contamination rates, with provable validity.
why: It would make corrupted laboratory and sensor tables usable for network discovery, where whole-row rejection would discard too much usable data.
key_works: Loh and Tan, 2015, “High-dimensional robust precision matrix estimation: Cellwise corruption under ε-contamination,” arXiv:1509.07229.

title: Adaptive bands with unknown anisotropic self-similarity
open: Construct honest, rate-adaptive confidence bands for anisotropic functions when smoothness differs by coordinate and the constants controlling self-similarity are unknown.
status: Honest adaptation is impossible over unrestricted nested smoothness classes; self-similarity permits positive results. The target is the sharp attainable anisotropic and locally varying extension.
why: It would permit uncertainty bands that adapt without hiding uncheckable tuning choices.
key_works: Bull, 2012, “Honest adaptive confidence bands and self-similar functions,” arXiv:1110.4985, DOI:10.1214/12-EJS720.

title: Confidence sets adapting to intrinsic dimension
open: When can a confidence set be honest without knowing the dimension or shape of the data's support? Determine which separation and geometric conditions permit confidence sets to adapt simultaneously to unknown smoothness, manifold dimension, and support geometry.
status: Adaptation results exist for fixed-dimensional function and distribution classes (e.g., Bull, 2012, "Honest adaptive confidence bands and self-similar functions"; Deo and Randrianarisoa, 2021, "On Adaptive Confidence Sets for the Wasserstein Distances," arXiv:2111.08505). Unknown geometry introduces additional indistinguishability boundaries that require explicit treatment, which existing theory does not provide.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the separation and geometric conditions under which honest, adaptive confidence sets over classes with unknown smoothness, intrinsic manifold dimension, and support geometry are possible, including explicit treatment of the indistinguishability boundaries that unknown geometry introduces.
why: It would justify dimension-adaptive uncertainty rather than only dimension-adaptive prediction.
key_works: Deo and Randrianarisoa, 2021, “On Adaptive Confidence Sets for the Wasserstein Distances,” arXiv:2111.08505; Bull, 2012, “Honest adaptive confidence bands and self-similar functions.”

title: Adaptive conditional-independence testing
open: Is there a test of conditional independence that adapts to unknown smoothness classes while remaining minimax-optimal? More precisely, the goal is to derive minimax testing rates and adaptive procedures for conditional independence over classes with unknown smoothness, sparse relevant conditioning variables, and explicitly bounded conditional densities.
status: Unrestricted conditional-independence testing has strong impossibility results, as shown by Shah and Peters, 2020, “The Hardness of Conditional Independence Testing and the Generalised Covariance Measure,” arXiv:1804.07203, DOI:10.1214/19-AOS1857. The open task is to identify sharp, useful restricted classes and the cost of adapting among them.
solved_when: Minimax testing rates are established for conditional independence over the restricted classes described (unknown smoothness, sparse relevant conditioning variables, explicitly bounded conditional densities), together with procedures that adapt across those classes at a quantified cost matching the minimax rates.
why: A solution would strengthen causal discovery and conditional association screening, replacing impossible general-purpose tests with sharp guarantees on realistic model classes.
key_works: Shah and Peters, 2020, “The Hardness of Conditional Independence Testing and the Generalised Covariance Measure,” arXiv:1804.07203, DOI:10.1214/19-AOS1857.

title: Power-optimal testing after learning the test representation
open: Can a two-sample test learn its kernel or representation directly from the observations being tested, while still controlling finite-sample error and achieving near-oracle power over specified alternative classes?
status: Sample splitting and adaptive-data-analysis techniques already provide valid approaches, so validity alone is settled; the sharper open target is the best achievable power–reuse tradeoff. Key references: Dwork et al., 2015, “Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis,” arXiv:1411.2664; Wasserman, Ramdas, and Balakrishnan, 2020, “Universal Inference,” arXiv:1912.11436.
solved_when: A testing procedure is given that both maintains valid finite-sample error control and attains near-oracle power over the specified alternative classes, with a characterization of the best achievable power–reuse tradeoff.
why: It would reduce the substantial power losses currently caused by reserving part of the data for representation learning, letting tests exploit all observations.
key_works: Dwork et al., 2015, “Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis,” arXiv:1411.2664; Wasserman, Ramdas, and Balakrishnan, 2020, “Universal Inference,” arXiv:1912.11436.

title: Entropy-rate estimation with unknown memory and mixing
open: How accurately can the entropy rate of a stochastic process be estimated when neither its memory length nor its mixing strength is known in advance? Formally, determine the minimax rates for entropy-rate estimation over processes with unknown finite memory and unknown mixing, together with procedures that adapt to both.
status: Sharp results exist for important stationary reversible Markov-chain classes (Han, Jiao, Lee, Weissman, Wu, and Yu, 2018, “Entropy Rate Estimation for Markov Chains with Large State Space,” arXiv:1802.07889). Unknown memory, growing state spaces, and adaptation across mixing regimes remain a distinct extension.
solved_when: Minimax estimation rates are established for entropy-rate estimation under unknown finite memory and unknown mixing strength, and estimators are given that adapt to both without prior knowledge of either.
why: A solution would yield principled complexity measurement for language, biological sequences, and telemetry, where memory length and mixing are rarely known in practice.
key_works: Han, Jiao, Lee, Weissman, Wu, and Yu, 2018, “Entropy Rate Estimation for Markov Chains with Large State Space,” arXiv:1802.07889.

title: Sharp risk of smoothed log-concave estimators
open: What are the sharp global and local risk guarantees for smoothed log-concave maximum-likelihood estimators, and does smoothing preserve the optimal adaptation these estimators enjoy for simpler densities?
status: Smoothed estimators have existed since at least 2013 — see Chen and Samworth, 2013, “Smoothed log-concave maximum likelihood estimation with applications,” arXiv:1102.1191, DOI:10.5705/ss.2011.224 — and their practical usefulness currently runs ahead of a complete sharp risk theory.
solved_when: Sharp (matching upper and lower bound) global and local risk results are established for smoothed log-concave MLEs, including a determination of whether smoothing preserves optimal adaptation to simpler density classes.
why: It would justify smoothed density and tail estimates on theoretical grounds rather than treating smoothing as a cosmetic post-processing step.
key_works: Chen and Samworth, 2013, “Smoothed log-concave maximum likelihood estimation with applications,” arXiv:1102.1191, DOI:10.5705/ss.2011.224.

title: Remaining logarithmic gaps in log-concave density risk
open: Are the logarithmic factors in current global Hellinger-risk bounds for multivariate log-concave maximum-likelihood estimation genuinely necessary, or can they be removed? Equivalently, determine the exact minimax rate (up to constants) for estimating a log-concave density in d dimensions under global Hellinger loss.
status: Dimension-dependent polynomial rates are known; the recent survey identifies remaining logarithmic discrepancies rather than an absence of minimax theory. Key works: Kim and Samworth, 2016, "Global rates of convergence in log-concave density estimation," arXiv:1404.2298, DOI:10.1214/16-AOS1480.
solved_when: Global Hellinger-risk bounds for multivariate log-concave MLE are established that either match the known dimension-dependent polynomial rates with no extraneous logarithmic factors, or a matching lower bound is proved showing the logarithmic factors cannot be removed.
why: It would complete one of shape-constrained statistics' central benchmark problems, settling the exact minimax rate for log-concave density estimation.
key_works: Kim and Samworth, 2016, “Global rates of convergence in log-concave density estimation,” arXiv:1404.2298, DOI:10.1214/16-AOS1480.

title: Certificates of unexplored posterior mass
subfield: Markov-chain Monte Carlo and posterior computation
open: Can we bound, in a computable way, how much posterior mass a finite set of MCMC chains might have left unexplored? More precisely, under explicit geometric assumptions on separated modes, construct computable upper bounds on the posterior mass that a finite collection of chains may have missed.
status: Standard convergence diagnostics cannot certify arbitrary undiscovered modes; the open target is useful certification under stated restrictions, not an impossible universal diagnostic. Key work: Vehtari et al., 2021, "Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: An improved R-hat for assessing convergence of MCMC," arXiv:1903.08008.
solved_when: An explicit geometric assumption on mode separation is stated, and under it a computable upper bound on undiscovered posterior mass is constructed and proven for finite collections of chains.
why: It would prevent seemingly converged chains from supporting confidently wrong decisions.
key_works: Vehtari et al., 2021, “Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: An improved R-hat for assessing convergence of MCMC,” arXiv:1903.08008.

title: Complexity theory for practical NUTS
subfield: Markov-chain Monte Carlo and posterior computation
open: Can we prove end-to-end sampling complexity bounds for the No-U-Turn sampler as it is actually used in practice? That is, for realistically adapted samplers incorporating step-size adaptation, mass-matrix learning, trajectory termination, and constrained parameter transformations.
status: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo has a substantial theoretical foundation; practical adaptive implementations combine mechanisms whose full guarantees require additional assumptions and analysis.
solved_when: A rigorous analysis establishes end-to-end complexity guarantees for a No-U-Turn sampler that includes step-size adaptation, mass-matrix learning, trajectory termination, and constrained parameter transformations.
why: It would explain when a standard Bayesian workhorse can be trusted to scale.
key_works: Betancourt, 2017, “A Conceptual Introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo,” arXiv:1701.02434.

title: Computable functional-bias bounds for variational inference
open: After fitting a variational approximation to a posterior, can we compute useful, rigorous bounds on the error in selected posterior expectations and tail probabilities — without knowing the exact posterior normalizing constant?
status: Variational objectives are tractable surrogates, but objective quality alone does not guarantee every scientific functional is accurate. The field is surveyed in Blei, Kucukelbir, and McAuliffe, 2017, “Variational Inference: A Review for Statisticians,” arXiv:1601.00670, DOI:10.1080/01621459.2017.1285773.
solved_when: A method exists that, given a fitted variational approximation, produces computable error bounds on chosen posterior expectations and tail probabilities, with no requirement of the exact posterior normalizing constant.
why: It would convert fast variational approximations into auditable inferential tools whose reported functionals carry certified accuracy.
key_works: Blei, Kucukelbir, and McAuliffe, 2017, “Variational Inference: A Review for Statisticians,” arXiv:1601.00670, DOI:10.1080/01621459.2017.1285773.

title: Complete admissibility theory for e-processes
open: When is an e-process admissible, in the sense that no other e-process uniformly dominates it, under a broad composite null? Give necessary and sufficient conditions, including a characterization of when one e-process uniformly improves another.
status: Martingale-based necessity results are established; the 2023 safe-inference survey lists broader admissibility questions. Ramdas, Ruf, Larsson, and Koolen, 2020, “Admissible anytime-valid sequential inference must rely on nonnegative martingales,” arXiv:2009.03167.
solved_when: Necessary and sufficient conditions for admissibility of e-processes under broad composite nulls are proven, including a full characterization of when one e-process uniformly improves another.
why: It would separate fundamentally efficient sequential evidence from avoidable conservatism, telling statisticians which anytime-valid procedures cannot be improved.
key_works: Ramdas, Ruf, Larsson, and Koolen, 2020, “Admissible anytime-valid sequential inference must rely on nonnegative martingales,” arXiv:2009.03167.

title: Sharp power theory for universal inference
open: When can universal-inference methods match the power and confidence-set accuracy of model-specific procedures? A full answer would characterize the best achievable power and confidence-set size for universal-inference constructions, including optimal splitting, aggregation, and nuisance fitting.
status: Finite-sample validity is established for broad likelihood-based settings; sharp efficiency relative to model-specific procedures remains open. Key work: Wasserman, Ramdas, and Balakrishnan, 2020, “Universal Inference,” arXiv:1912.11436.
solved_when: A sharp characterization of the best achievable power and confidence-set size for universal-inference constructions is obtained, covering optimal splitting, aggregation, and nuisance fitting — that is, matching efficiency lower and upper bounds relative to model-specific procedures.
why: It would show when broad applicability costs little in efficiency and when it is prohibitively conservative, telling practitioners exactly when universal methods are safe to rely on.
key_works: Wasserman, Ramdas, and Balakrishnan, 2020, “Universal Inference,” arXiv:1912.11436.

title: Model-X inference with learned covariate distributions
open: Can model-X knockoff methods retain sharp false-discovery-rate control when the covariate distribution used to generate knockoffs is itself learned from data, with the resulting uncertainty adapting to where the misspecification actually matters?
status: Model-X knockoffs provide guarantees under appropriate distributional knowledge of the covariates; robustness to estimated conditional laws is an active extension rather than an automatic consequence of existing theory. Founding work: Candès, Fan, Janson, and Lv, 2018, “Panning for Gold: Model-X Knockoffs for High-dimensional Controlled Variable Selection,” arXiv:1610.02351.
solved_when: A method is given that provably controls the false discovery rate under learned (imperfectly specified) covariate distributions, with guarantees that are sharp and adapt to the regions of covariate space where misspecification affects validity.
why: It would free conditional variable discovery from dependence on an unverifiable generative model for the covariates, making controlled selection usable in practice.
key_works: Candès, Fan, Janson, and Lv, 2018, “Panning for Gold: Model-X Knockoffs for High-dimensional Controlled Variable Selection,” arXiv:1610.02351.

title: Error control for adaptively constructed hypothesis hierarchies
open: Can we control false discoveries simultaneously across all levels of a hypothesis hierarchy when the grouping structure itself is learned adaptively from the same data on which the tests are run? Formally, the goal is valid error control for testing over a data-dependently chosen tree (or partial order) of groups and subgroups, rather than a pre-specified hierarchy.
status: This is an open research target combining structured multiple testing with adaptive data analysis. A fixed, pre-specified hierarchy is materially simpler than one chosen to make discoveries look coherent. Related work includes Dwork et al., 2015, "Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis," arXiv:1411.2664, and Wang and Ramdas, 2022, "False discovery rate control with e-values"; neighboring areas are adaptive query trees in computer science and data-driven ontology discovery in bioinformatics.
solved_when: A testing procedure is given that, when the hierarchy of groups and subgroups is constructed from the same data used for testing, provably controls the false discovery rate (or another stated error measure) simultaneously across all levels of the hierarchy.
why: It would make pathway, ontology, and subgroup discovery reliable, since these pipelines currently report structures whose apparent coherence may be an artifact of the adaptive construction.
key_works: Dwork et al., 2015, “Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis,” arXiv:1411.2664; Wang and Ramdas, 2022, “False discovery rate control with e-values.”

title: Selective inference after deep clustering
subfield: Selective inference and adaptive data analysis
open: When a deep neural network has learned a nonlinear representation and produced clusters — with the architecture, the number of clusters, and the comparisons all chosen adaptively from the same data — can we still derive valid uncertainty quantification for differences between those clusters? Formally, this asks for selective inference that remains valid under a much more complicated, data-dependent selection event than current exact methods handle.
status: Exact selective methods exist for tractable selection events, notably Lee et al., 2016, "Exact post-selection inference, with application to the lasso," arXiv:1311.6238, and Dwork et al., 2015, "Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis." Deep clustering generally produces a much more complicated data-dependent event that these methods do not cover.
solved_when: A method is derived that provides valid (e.g., exact or valid p-values/confidence intervals) inference for between-cluster differences, accounting for selection of the architecture, the cluster count, and the chosen comparison.
why: It would prevent algorithmically manufactured groups from generating spurious scientific findings.
key_works: Lee et al., 2016, “Exact post-selection inference, with application to the lasso,” arXiv:1311.6238; Dwork et al., 2015, “Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis.”

title: Inference over analyst-selected multiverses
subfield: Selective inference and adaptive data analysis
open: How should we quantify uncertainty when analysts explore many defensible specifications of the same data and report only a chosen subset, without assuming the set of specifications was fixed in advance?
status: Many-analyst studies demonstrate substantial analytic variability; see Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020, "Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams," DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9. Related theory appears in Dwork et al., 2015, "Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis." The target is valid inference for adaptive exploration, not merely displaying a specification curve.
solved_when: A method exists that yields valid inference (e.g., calibrated confidence intervals or error control) for adaptively selected subsets of specifications, addressing the variability that many-analyst studies demonstrate, rather than merely displaying a specification curve.
why: It would make robustness analysis resistant to its own selection bias, restoring trust in findings assembled after adaptive exploration.
key_works: Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020, “Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams,” DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9; Dwork et al., 2015, “Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis.”

title: Cross-validation uncertainty under weak algorithmic stability
subfield: Selective inference and adaptive data analysis
open: Can we construct informative confidence intervals for prediction risk after cross-validation-based model selection, even when the learner is unstable and the data dependence is weak? Formally, the goal is intervals valid under explicitly weak stability and dependence assumptions.
status: There is no universally unbiased estimator of K-fold cross-validation variance, as shown by Bengio and Grandvalet, 2004, "No Unbiased Estimator of the Variance of K-Fold Cross-Validation," JMLR 5:1089–1105. That negative result does not settle restricted, calibrated intervals for modern unstable learners.
solved_when: A procedure producing calibrated confidence intervals for post-cross-validation prediction risk is shown to be valid under explicitly weak stability and dependence assumptions, going beyond the negative result that no universally unbiased estimator of K-fold cross-validation variance exists.
why: It would make reported differences between predictive models more trustworthy.
key_works: Bengio and Grandvalet, 2004, “No Unbiased Estimator of the Variance of K-Fold Cross-Validation,” JMLR 5:1089–1105.

title: Conditional coverage versus prediction-set size
open: In distribution-free prediction, how much must prediction-set size grow if we demand coverage that holds not just on average but approximately across subpopulations? Formally, determine sharp achievable tradeoffs among approximate conditional coverage, the complexity of the conditioning family, and expected prediction-set volume.
status: Exact unrestricted distribution-free conditional coverage is already ruled out in useful settings; the open problem concerns nontrivial restricted or approximate guarantees. Key work: Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani, 2019/2021, “The limits of distribution-free conditional predictive inference,” arXiv:1903.04684. Related lines include multigroup calibration in learning theory and uncertainty quantification for small subpopulations in fairness.
solved_when: Sharp (matching upper and lower bound) tradeoff curves are established relating the permitted approximation error in conditional coverage, the complexity of the conditioning class, and the expected prediction-set volume.
why: It would clarify what “reliable for people like this” can actually mean — which subpopulation-level coverage guarantees are achievable without inflating prediction sets unboundedly.
key_works: Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani, 2019/2021, “The limits of distribution-free conditional predictive inference,” arXiv:1903.04684.

title: Conformal prediction with uncertain shift weights
open: Can we give sharp finite-sample coverage guarantees for conformal prediction when the covariate-shift importance weights are themselves estimated and possibly misspecified, especially in low-overlap regions where they become unstable?
status: Weighted and doubly robust calibration methods exist, but no complete finite-sample treatment of uncertainty in the weights themselves is available. Key works: Yang, Kuchibhotla, and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2024, “Doubly robust calibration of prediction sets under covariate shift,” JRSS B 86:943–965; Barber et al., 2023, “Conformal prediction beyond exchangeability,” arXiv:2202.13415.
solved_when: A complete finite-sample uncertainty accounting for the weights exists — i.e., coverage bounds that hold when the importance weights are estimated, allow misspecification, and remain valid under instability in low-overlap regions.
why: It would improve the reliability of prediction sets after deployment, when the population has shifted from the training distribution.
key_works: Yang, Kuchibhotla, and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2024, “Doubly robust calibration of prediction sets under covariate shift,” JRSS B 86:943–965; Barber et al., 2023, “Conformal prediction beyond exchangeability,” arXiv:2202.13415.

title: Minimal validation designs for causal measurement error
open: Which combinations of repeated measurements, validation subsamples, and randomized measurement devices suffice to identify causal effects when measurement errors are nonlinear and correlated? More precisely, is there a characterization of the measurement designs under which causal effects remain identifiable despite dependent, nonlinear error structures?
status: Proxy-variable identification supplies useful special cases, notably Miao, Geng, and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2018, “Identifying causal effects with proxy variables of an unmeasured confounder,” and Tchetgen Tchetgen et al., 2020, “An Introduction to Proximal Causal Learning,” arXiv:2009.10982; a design-level characterization for dependent errors remains a more specific outstanding target.
solved_when: A complete design-level characterization exists of the measurement-design combinations (repeated measurements, validation subsamples, randomized measurement devices) that identify causal effects under nonlinear and correlated errors.
why: It would tell investigators which additional measurements are actually worth collecting before a study is fielded, instead of collecting data that fails to identify the target effect.
key_works: Miao, Geng, and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2018, “Identifying causal effects with proxy variables of an unmeasured confounder”; Tchetgen Tchetgen et al., 2020, “An Introduction to Proximal Causal Learning,” arXiv:2009.10982.

title: Heterogeneous-effect inference under weak overlap
open: When treated and control populations barely overlap and we do not know how smooth the treatment effect is as a function of covariates, can we still produce honest confidence bands for conditional treatment effects? Formally, derive minimax confidence bands for conditional treatment effects under overlap that deteriorates with sample size and unknown effect smoothness.
status: Flexible treatment-effect estimation is mature in important regimes, but uniform uncertainty quantification, bias adaptation, and weak overlap interact in ways not settled by prediction rates alone; the problem is listed among open challenges in Cinelli et al., 2025, "Challenges in Statistics: A Dozen Challenges in Causality and Causal Inference," arXiv:2508.17099, while honest adaptive confidence bands for self-similar functions were studied by Bull, 2012, "Honest adaptive confidence bands and self-similar functions."
solved_when: A construction of confidence bands for conditional treatment effects is given that is minimax — achieving valid coverage and optimal width — in the regime where overlap deteriorates with sample size and effect smoothness is unknown, with the rates certified.
why: It would identify which personalized treatment recommendations are actually supported by data, separating reliable individualized conclusions from extrapolation in regions where data is thin.
key_works: Cinelli et al., 2025, “Challenges in Statistics: A Dozen Challenges in Causality and Causal Inference,” arXiv:2508.17099; Bull, 2012, “Honest adaptive confidence bands and self-similar functions.”

title: Policy-value inference after learning under interference
open: When treatments spill over across a network and the allocation policy is itself learned from the same network data, how can we obtain valid confidence bounds for that policy's value? Formally, the goal is post-selection inference for the value of a learned treatment-allocation policy in the presence of interference.
status: Policy learning and randomization-based interference inference have substantial separate literatures; their joint post-selection problem is more demanding and remains open. Key works: Aronow and Samii, 2017, “Estimating Average Causal Effects Under General Interference, with Application to a Social Network Experiment,” arXiv:1305.6156; Athey and Wager, 2021, “Policy Learning With Observational Data.”
solved_when: A method exists that delivers provably valid confidence bounds for the value of a policy learned from network data on which one unit's treatment affects others, accounting for the selection step.
why: It would support defensible rollout of network-wide interventions, where naive confidence statements can be invalidated by both interference and selection.
key_works: Aronow and Samii, 2017, “Estimating Average Causal Effects Under General Interference, with Application to a Social Network Experiment,” arXiv:1305.6156; Athey and Wager, 2021, “Policy Learning With Observational Data.”

title: Learning the exposure mapping
open: Can we still identify — or at least partially identify — causal effects when the exposure mapping itself, the rule translating neighbors' treatment assignments into an individual's effective exposure, is unknown and must be learned from data?
status: General-interference frameworks typically take the exposure mapping as given by the analyst; estimating that mapping without invalidating inference remains a distinct, unresolved component. A key framework is Aronow and Samii, 2017, “Estimating Average Causal Effects Under General Interference,” arXiv:1305.6156. Related threads appear in network science (learning influence neighborhoods) and causal discovery (interaction-structure identification).
solved_when: A method is given that learns the exposure mapping and supports valid (or partially identifying) inference for causal effects under general interference, without the inference being invalidated by the estimation of the mapping itself.
why: It would reduce dependence on arbitrary definitions of spillover exposure, letting interference analyses proceed without hand-specified exposure rules.
key_works: Aronow and Samii, 2017, “Estimating Average Causal Effects Under General Interference,” arXiv:1305.6156.

title: Sharp bounds for interacting multiple mediators
open: When several mediators act between a treatment and an outcome, can we compute sharp bounds on the effect attributable to each mechanism when the mediators interact, their causal ordering is only partly known, and mediator–outcome confounding cannot be ruled out?
status: Mediation estimands and identification strategies are established (VanderWeele, 2015, *Explanation in Causal Inference: Methods for Mediation and Interaction*), but the combination of uncertain ordering, mediator interactions, and explicit partial identification remains open; it is flagged as a challenge in Cinelli et al., 2025, "A Dozen Challenges in Causality and Causal Inference," arXiv:2508.17099.
solved_when: Computable, sharp (i.e., non-improvable) bounds are derived for mechanism-specific effects under multiple interacting mediators with partially unknown ordering and possible mediator–outcome confounding.
why: It would let researchers distinguish plausible mechanisms from data without pretending that all pathway assumptions are known.
key_works: VanderWeele, 2015, *Explanation in Causal Inference: Methods for Mediation and Interaction*; Cinelli et al., 2025, “A Dozen Challenges in Causality and Causal Inference,” arXiv:2508.17099.

title: Switchback experiments with unknown carryover
open: Can we jointly design switchback schedules and estimate treatment effects when the duration of carryover is unknown, possibly heterogeneous across units, and of the same order as the experiment itself? In formal terms, this asks for a procedure that adapts the randomization schedule and quantifies uncertainty without knowing the persistence structure of past treatments.
status: Online experimentation has developed many specialized designs, but unknown carryover makes both randomization choice and uncertainty calibration harder. A broad review of the area's statistical challenges is Larsen et al., 2024, “Statistical challenges in online controlled experiments: A review of A/B testing methodology,” *The American Statistician* 78:135–149.
solved_when: A method exists that jointly selects switching schedules and delivers valid treatment-effect estimates with calibrated uncertainty when carryover duration is unknown, heterogeneous, and comparable to the experimental horizon.
why: It would improve experiments in marketplaces, logistics, and shared infrastructure, where interference from earlier treatments is the norm rather than the exception.
key_works: Larsen et al., 2024, “Statistical challenges in online controlled experiments: A review of A/B testing methodology,” *The American Statistician* 78:135–149.

title: Downstream inference with uncertain entity linkage
subfield: Missing data, measurement error, and record linkage
open: When records are linked across databases with uncertainty, how should we construct confidence intervals for regression coefficients and causal estimands that honestly account for the possibility that the links themselves are wrong? In particular, the intervals should integrate over the distribution of possible linkages, including the case where linkage quality depends on the outcome.
status: Probabilistic linkage and entity resolution are mature topics (see Binette and Steorts, 2022, “(Almost) All of Entity Resolution,” arXiv:2008.04443, DOI:10.1126/sciadv.abi8021), but it remains standard to treat one estimated linkage as truth, which can omit a material source of uncertainty. Related threads exist in uncertain joins in databases and privacy-preserving record linkage.
solved_when: A method exists that produces valid confidence intervals for regression and causal estimands integrating linkage uncertainty, including dependence between linkage quality and the outcome.
why: It would improve the reliability of inference drawn from linked administrative and health records.
key_works: Binette and Steorts, 2022, “(Almost) All of Entity Resolution,” arXiv:2008.04443, DOI:10.1126/sciadv.abi8021.

title: Imputation valid for adaptively chosen analyses
subfield: Missing data, measurement error, and record linkage
open: Can one build imputation procedures whose uncertainty guarantees survive the way analysts actually use completed data — that is, analyses chosen after looking at the imputed values? Formally, develop imputation procedures and uncertainty rules that remain valid for a declared class of downstream analyses selected after inspecting the imputed data.
status: This is a proposed target extending congeniality and adaptive-analysis concerns; no solution exists. The state of the art establishes that validity for one prespecified analysis does not establish validity for an unrestricted analytic search. Key works: Dwork et al., 2015, “Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis,” arXiv:1411.2664; Gelman et al., 2020, “Bayesian Workflow,” arXiv:2011.01808.
solved_when: An imputation procedure is constructed together with uncertainty rules whose validity holds over a declared class of downstream analyses, including those chosen after inspection of the imputed data — not merely for a single prespecified analysis.
why: It would make reusable completed datasets less likely to produce undercovered conclusions, addressing the gap between validity for one prespecified analysis and validity under an unrestricted analytic search.
key_works: Dwork et al., 2015, “Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis,” arXiv:1411.2664; Gelman et al., 2020, “Bayesian Workflow,” arXiv:2011.01808.

title: Efficient sample-optimal pure-private sparse means
open: Can sparse Gaussian mean estimation achieve its information-theoretically optimal sample complexity under pure differential privacy by a polynomial-time algorithm, or does pure privacy create a fundamental computational gap here? Formally: give a poly-time pure-DP estimator matching the optimal sample complexity, or prove a matching computational barrier.
status: The problem was explicitly highlighted in a 2025 robust-statistics open-problem lecture (UW CSE 599K, 2025, “Lecture 18”). Privacy-induced computational gaps are already established in related sparse estimation settings (Georgiev and Hopkins, 2022, “Privacy Induces Robustness: Information-Computation Gaps and Sparse Mean Estimation,” arXiv:2211.00724).
solved_when: Either a polynomial-time, pure differentially private algorithm for sparse Gaussian mean estimation attains the information-theoretically optimal sample complexity, or a matching computational lower bound is established showing no such efficient algorithm exists.
why: A positive answer would make strong privacy guarantees practical for high-dimensional population estimation; a barrier would clarify where privacy fundamentally trades off against computation.
key_works: Georgiev and Hopkins, 2022, “Privacy Induces Robustness: Information-Computation Gaps and Sparse Mean Estimation,” arXiv:2211.00724; UW CSE 599K, 2025, “Lecture 18.”

title: Change-point intervals after choosing the number of changes
open: Can we construct confidence intervals for the locations of change-points that remain simultaneously valid even after the number, scale, and type of changes has been chosen from the data, in settings with dependent noise?
status: Sharp localization theory exists for important independent mean-change models (Wang, Yu, and Rinaldo, 2018/2020, “Univariate Mean Change Point Detection: Penalization, CUSUM and Optimality,” arXiv:1810.09498), but full post-selection coverage is a stronger requirement; exact post-selection inference is available in related settings (Lee et al., 2016, “Exact post-selection inference”).
solved_when: A procedure exists that provides simultaneous location intervals with guaranteed post-selection coverage when the number, scale, and type of changes are data-driven and the errors are dependent.
why: It would attach defensible, quantified dates to inferred regime changes rather than point estimates whose uncertainty is invalidated by the model-selection step.
key_works: Wang, Yu, and Rinaldo, 2018/2020, “Univariate Mean Change Point Detection: Penalization, CUSUM and Optimality,” arXiv:1810.09498; Lee et al., 2016, “Exact post-selection inference.”

title: Computational limits of covariance change detection
open: When both the pre-change covariance and the change time are unknown, where do the statistical and polynomial-time detection boundaries lie for sparse changes in covariance? Formally, determine the detection boundary — and whether a gap separates it from what polynomial-time algorithms can achieve — for sparse covariance changes in this doubly-unknown setting.
status: This is a proposed target connecting high-dimensional change detection with sparse spectral hardness; no detection boundaries are yet established. Mean-change theory alone does not characterize the problem. Related key works include Berthet and Rigollet, 2013, "Complexity Theoretic Lower Bounds for Sparse Principal Component Detection," and Wang et al., "Univariate Mean Change Point Detection," arXiv:1810.09498. Applications motivating the problem include cybersecurity detection of coordinated anomalies and connections to complexity-theoretic sparse spectral detection.
solved_when: Characterizations of both the statistical detection boundary and the polynomial-time detection boundary for sparse covariance changes with unknown pre-change covariance and unknown change time are established, in particular clarifying whether a statistical–computational gap arises.
why: A solution would reveal when monitoring altered relationships among variables requires more data than detecting altered averages, since mean-change theory alone does not characterize this problem.
key_works: Berthet and Rigollet, 2013, “Complexity Theoretic Lower Bounds for Sparse Principal Component Detection”; Wang et al., “Univariate Mean Change Point Detection,” arXiv:1810.09498.

title: Microergodicity in nonstationary anisotropic models
open: Which covariance functionals can actually be consistently estimated when we observe a nonstationary, anisotropic, or multivariate spatial process on a fixed, bounded domain? More formally, classify the microergodic (fixed-domain identifiable) parameter functionals for useful nonstationary, anisotropic, and multivariate spatial models.
status: Microergodic parameters are understood in important stationary families, including recent work such as Zhang, Tang, and Banerjee, 2024, “Fixed-Domain Asymptotics Under Vecchia’s Approximation of Spatial Process Likelihoods”; generalizing the identifiable parameter, rather than assuming all covariance parameters are estimable, remains essential. Background for the area appears in Moraga, 2023, *Spatial Statistics for Data Science: Theory and Practice with R*.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the covariance functionals that are consistently identifiable under fixed-domain asymptotics for these model classes, replacing the assumption that all covariance parameters are estimable with a general account of the identifiable parameter.
why: It would stop spatial models from attaching artificial certainty to nonidentifiable parameters.
key_works: Zhang, Tang, and Banerjee, 2024, “Fixed-Domain Asymptotics Under Vecchia’s Approximation of Spatial Process Likelihoods”; Moraga, 2023, *Spatial Statistics for Data Science: Theory and Practice with R*.

title: Honest adaptation across tail classes
open: When can a confidence interval for an extreme quantile adapt to an unknown tail class and unknown second-order bias while still maintaining honest, uniform coverage? In other words, under what conditions does adaptation to the severity of the tail not force a loss of coverage guarantees over the whole class of distributions?
status: Proposed as a frontier formulation. The central obstacle identified is the indistinguishability between distributions that agree over observed ranges but differ in remote tails, which any adaptation scheme must confront. Related literature includes Engelke and Ivanovs, 2021, “Sparse Structures for Multivariate Extremes,” arXiv:2004.12182, and Bull, 2012, “Honest adaptive confidence bands and self-similar functions.”
solved_when: A characterization is given — necessary and sufficient conditions on the tail classes and second-order parameters — under which confidence intervals for extreme quantiles adapt to the unknown tail class and second-order bias while retaining uniform coverage, together with an interval construction achieving (or provably逼近) that boundary.
why: It would make extrapolation of rare-event risk credible: practitioners could report extreme loss quantiles whose coverage holds honestly across tail behaviors, rather than intervals that are valid only under assumed tail conditions.
key_works: Engelke and Ivanovs, 2021, “Sparse Structures for Multivariate Extremes,” arXiv:2004.12182; Bull, 2012, “Honest adaptive confidence bands and self-similar functions.”

title: Graphs mixing asymptotic dependence and independence
open: Can one build a multivariate tail model that is sparse, identifiable, and allows different pairs or subsets of variables to display asymptotic dependence or asymptotic independence simultaneously? In formal terms, the goal is a joint tail distribution that mixes these regimes coherently while carrying valid structure uncertainty.
status: Sparse extremal models are well developed in important regimes, notably via Engelke and Ivanovs, 2021, “Sparse Structures for Multivariate Extremes,” arXiv:2004.12182. Combining dependence and independence regimes without producing incoherent joint distributions remains a continuing frontier.
solved_when: An identifiable sparse multivariate tail model is constructed that accommodates asymptotic dependence and asymptotic independence across different pairs or subsets within a single coherent joint distribution, together with valid quantification of structure uncertainty.
why: It would better represent compound risks — such as climate compound extremes — whose variables do not share one universal tail-dependence pattern.
key_works: Engelke and Ivanovs, 2021, “Sparse Structures for Multivariate Extremes,” arXiv:2004.12182.

title: Efficient inference in hard stochastic-block-model phases
open: When a sparse stochastic block model has many communities, can the information contained in the network be recovered in polynomial time even in regimes where detection is information-theoretically possible but no efficient algorithm is known? Formally, resolve the polynomial-time detectability frontier in sparse block models with sufficiently many groups, where the information-theoretic and algorithmic thresholds separate.
status: Thresholds are settled in important two-community and other special regimes, but those successes do not eliminate the harder multi-community phases. See Abbe, 2017/2018, “Community Detection and Stochastic Block Models: Recent Developments,” arXiv:1703.10146.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the regimes (in sparsity and number of communities) in which polynomial-time algorithms achieve detection, matching or provably failing to match the information-theoretic threshold.
why: It would clarify when community information is present in a network yet computationally inaccessible, delineating the gap between what the data supports and what efficient computation can extract.
key_works: Abbe, 2017/2018, “Community Detection and Stochastic Block Models: Recent Developments,” arXiv:1703.10146.

title: Uncertainty for overlapping multilayer communities
open: Can we infer the number of communities, their overlap structure, and their alignment across layers — with honest, calibrated uncertainty — in a multilayer network whose layers differ in sparsity and share only some of their nodes? Formally, this asks for a procedure that jointly quantifies uncertainty over community count, overlap memberships, and cross-layer correspondence rather than fixing any of them in advance.
status: Proposed target extending block-model and shared-subspace methods; fixed community count and complete layer alignment are materially easier. Key works: Abbe, "Community Detection and Stochastic Block Models"; Lock et al., 2013, "Joint and individual variation explained," arXiv:1102.4110.
solved_when: A method exists that recovers the number of communities, the overlapping memberships, and the cross-layer alignment with calibrated uncertainty, valid when layers differ in sparsity and share only a subset of nodes.
why: It would make multilayer community findings less dependent on arbitrary modeling choices, replacing assumptions about community count and layer alignment with quantified evidence.
key_works: Abbe, “Community Detection and Stochastic Block Models”; Lock et al., 2013, “Joint and individual variation explained,” arXiv:1102.4110.

title: Functional regression with unknown ill-posedness
open: Can we construct confidence sets for functional regression coefficients that remain honest when both the decay rate of the predictor covariance eigenvalues and the smoothness of the coefficient are unknown? Formally, this asks for adaptive inference — coverage guarantees that hold simultaneously over a range of ill-posedness regimes without prior knowledge of either parameter.
status: Estimation and regularization theory provide a baseline, but simultaneous adaptation of uncertainty to unknown ill-posedness is more restrictive and remains unresolved. Relevant background includes Morris, 2015, “Functional Regression,” arXiv:1406.4068 and Ray, “Adaptive Bernstein–von Mises theorems in Gaussian white noise,” arXiv:1407.3397.
solved_when: A procedure is given whose confidence sets achieve honest, adaptive coverage for the functional regression coefficient over classes of covariance eigenvalue decays and coefficient smoothness that are both unknown to the analyst.
why: It would make functional regression error bars less dependent on fixed truncation assumptions, giving practitioners uncertainty statements they can trust without correctly guessing spectral decay or smoothness in advance.
key_works: Morris, 2015, “Functional Regression,” arXiv:1406.4068; Ray, “Adaptive Bernstein–von Mises theorems in Gaussian white noise,” arXiv:1407.3397.

title: Minimax conditional-independence testing for functional data
open: Given random functions with known spectral and smoothness structure, can we test conditional independence at provably optimal rates? In particular, what are the sharp minimax separation rates for such tests, and can they be achieved adaptively when the effective dimension of the functions is unknown?
status: Hilbert-space conditional-independence methods exist (Lundborg et al., 2022, DOI:10.1111/rssb.12544), but the current target is an optimal, adaptive theory rather than unrestricted testing, which faces impossibility in light of the hardness results of Shah and Peters, 2020, “The Hardness of Conditional Independence Testing and the Generalised Covariance Measure,” arXiv:1804.07203.
solved_when: Sharp minimax testing rates for conditional independence among random functions are established under explicit spectral and smoothness restrictions, including procedures that adapt to the unknown effective dimension.
why: It would put functional graphical models and dynamic biological pathway analysis on firm, optimal-theory footing rather than heuristic tests.
key_works: Shah and Peters, 2020, “The Hardness of Conditional Independence Testing and the Generalised Covariance Measure,” arXiv:1804.07203; Lundborg et al., 2022, Hilbert-space conditional-independence work, DOI:10.1111/rssb.12544.

title: Multistate models with informative intermittent observation
open: Can we consistently estimate transition intensities and state-occupation probabilities in a multistate model when panel observations are intermittent, the timing of visits depends on the hidden state, and recurrent transitions between visits go unrecorded? Formally, the goal is a framework that handles informative observation times together with unobserved transitions within a single multistate process.
status: Multistate and recurrent-event models provide a foundation, but jointly modeling informative observation and unobserved transitions remains a demanding extension. Key works: Andersen and Keiding, 2002, "Multistate models for event history analysis"; Beyersmann et al., 2012, *Competing Risks and Multistate Models with R*.
solved_when: A method exists that identifies and consistently estimates transition intensities and state-occupation probabilities under intermittent observation with state-dependent visit timing and possibly missed recurrent transitions.
why: It would improve the analysis of disease progression in clinical studies and of degradation in repairable systems, where visit times are rarely ignorable.
key_works: Andersen and Keiding, 2002, “Multistate models for event history analysis”; Beyersmann et al., 2012, *Competing Risks and Multistate Models with R*.

title: Fine-mapping uncertainty under LD-reference mismatch
subfield: Statistical genetics, omics, and microbiome analysis
open: Can we construct credible or confidence sets for causal variants that stay calibrated when the linkage disequilibrium reference panel differs from the actual study population? In particular, the sets should remain valid under reference mismatch and when rare variants are incompletely represented in the panel.
status: Statistical fine-mapping is mature, but reference mismatch and unresolved correlated variants remain important limitations (Schaid, Chen, and Larson, 2018, "From genome-wide associations to candidate causal variants by statistical fine-mapping," DOI:10.1038/s41576-018-0016-z).
solved_when: A method exists that constructs credible or confidence sets for causal variants with provable calibration (correct coverage) despite LD-reference mismatch between panel and study population and incomplete representation of rare variants.
why: It would improve the reliability of variant prioritization for downstream biological experiments, which currently rests on fine-mapping results whose uncertainty may be misstated.
key_works: Schaid, Chen, and Larson, 2018, “From genome-wide associations to candidate causal variants by statistical fine-mapping,” DOI:10.1038/s41576-018-0016-z.

title: Cross-population polygenic-score uncertainty
subfield: Statistical genetics, omics, and microbiome analysis
open: How can we quantify the uncertainty of polygenic-score predictions for individuals and subgroups when the scores are transferred across populations that differ in allele frequencies, linkage patterns, environments, and ascertainment? In formal terms, the goal is a theory of calibrated uncertainty — with transport diagnostics — for cross-population genetic prediction, rather than merely improved average accuracy.
status: Transferability failures and unequal predictive performance across populations are documented; the target is calibrated uncertainty and transport diagnostics, not merely improved average accuracy. Martin et al., 2019, "Clinical use of current polygenic risk scores may exacerbate health disparities," DOI:10.1038/s41588-019-0379-x.
solved_when: A framework exists that provides calibrated individual- and subgroup-level prediction uncertainty for polygenic scores applied across populations with different allele frequencies, linkage patterns, environments, and ascertainment, together with diagnostics for when transport across populations is reliable.
why: It would make genetic prediction less likely to amplify unequal evidential support across populations.
key_works: Martin et al., 2019, “Clinical use of current polygenic risk scores may exacerbate health disparities,” DOI:10.1038/s41588-019-0379-x.

title: Barker sequences longer than thirteen
open: Can a binary sequence whose off-peak autocorrelations are all at most 1 in absolute value — a Barker sequence — have length greater than thirteen? The problem asks for a proof that no such sequence exists, or an explicit construction of one.
status: Odd lengths beyond thirteen are excluded; the unresolved even-length case is connected to circulant Hadamard matrices, and large numerical exclusions do not settle all lengths. Key works: Turyn and Storer, 1961, "On binary sequences"; Leung and Schmidt, 2005, "The field descent method"; Leung and Schmidt, 2012, "New restrictions on possible orders of circulant Hadamard matrices."
solved_when: Either a proof that no binary Barker sequence of any length exceeding thirteen exists, or an explicit binary Barker sequence of length greater than thirteen, is produced.
why: It would resolve an extremal low-autocorrelation design problem, with direct ties to low-sidelobe radar waveforms and cyclic difference sets.
key_works: Turyn and Storer, 1961, “On binary sequences”; Leung and Schmidt, 2005, “The field descent method”; Leung and Schmidt, 2012, “New restrictions on possible orders of circulant Hadamard matrices.”

title: Projective plane of order twelve
open: Does a finite projective plane of order twelve exist? Equivalently, does a symmetric \(2\!-\!(157,13,1)\) design exist?
status: A classical unresolved finite-geometry existence problem. The necessary arithmetic conditions do not rule out order twelve. Key works: Elkies, 2015, Harvard Math 155 finite-geometry notes; classical projective-plane and balanced-design literature.
solved_when: A projective plane of order twelve is exhibited, or its nonexistence is proved; equivalently, a symmetric \(2\!-\!(157,13,1)\) design is constructed or shown not to exist.
why: A resolution would clarify the limits of highly balanced incidence designs, marking where such extremal symmetry can and cannot occur.
key_works: Elkies, 2015, Harvard Math 155 finite-geometry notes; classical projective-plane and balanced-design literature.

title: Full transversals in odd-order Latin squares
open: Does every Latin square of odd order have a full transversal — a selection of cells meeting every row, every column, and every symbol exactly once? In other words, is Ryser's conjecture true that odd order alone guarantees such a transversal?
status: This is Ryser's 1967 formulation of the full-transversal conjecture, and it remains open; known results on near-transversals do not settle the full odd-order statement. Surveys and data compilations include Wanless, 2011, "Transversals in Latin squares: a survey" (bibliographic details to verify) and Wanless, "Data on transversals in Latin squares."
solved_when: A proof that every Latin square of odd order admits a transversal containing one cell from each row, column, and symbol, or a counterexample of an odd-order Latin square with no such transversal.
why: It would strengthen existence guarantees for balanced selections in combinatorial designs, connecting to rainbow perfect matchings and balanced assignment problems.
key_works: Ryser, 1967, formulation; Wanless, 2011, “Transversals in Latin squares: a survey” (verify bibliographic details); Wanless, “Data on transversals in Latin squares.”

title: Hadamard matrices of every admissible order
open: Does a Hadamard matrix exist for every positive order divisible by four?
status: A classical unresolved existence conjecture with many infinite constructions and extensive computational progress; historical lists of the smallest missing orders should not be treated as current records. Key works: Hadamard, 1893, determinant work; "Quaternionic Perfect Sequences and Hadamard Matrices," 2026, arXiv:2601.22337; OEIS A007299 for evolving existence records.
solved_when: A proof that a Hadamard matrix exists for every positive multiple of four, or a disproof exhibiting an admissible order with no Hadamard matrix.
why: It would complete a basic existence foundation for orthogonal two-level designs and coding constructions.
key_works: Hadamard, 1893, determinant work; “Quaternionic Perfect Sequences and Hadamard Matrices,” 2026, arXiv:2601.22337; OEIS A007299 for evolving existence records.

title: Nonexistence of larger circulant Hadamard matrices
open: Is the 4×4 matrix the only nontrivial circulant Hadamard matrix in existence? Equivalently, prove or disprove that no circulant Hadamard matrix of order greater than four exists.
status: A longstanding conjecture, also known as the circulant Hadamard conjecture or Ryser's circulant Hadamard conjecture. Strong arithmetic restrictions exclude many possible orders — notably those of Leung and Schmidt, 2012, "New restrictions on possible orders of circulant Hadamard matrices," DOI:10.1007/s10623-011-9493-1 — but no all-orders proof is known. Related work includes "Quaternionic Perfect Sequences and Hadamard Matrices," 2026, arXiv:2601.22337.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) establishing that the only nontrivial circulant Hadamard matrices have order four, covering all orders.
why: It would settle a highly structured class of orthogonal sequence designs, with direct ties to perfect periodic binary sequences in signal processing.
key_works: Leung and Schmidt, 2012, “New restrictions on possible orders of circulant Hadamard matrices,” DOI:10.1007/s10623-011-9493-1; “Quaternionic Perfect Sequences and Hadamard Matrices,” 2026, arXiv:2601.22337.
aliases: Circulant Hadamard conjecture; Ryser’s circulant Hadamard conjecture.

title: Three mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order ten
open: Do there exist three pairwise mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order ten? Either exhibit such a triple or prove that none exists.
status: This is a specific longstanding design problem. Myrvold (1999, "Negative results for orthogonal triples of Latin squares of order 10") gave early negative results, and recent SAT work by Bright, Keita, and Stevens (2026, "Myrvold's results on orthogonal triples of 10×10 Latin squares: A SAT investigation," DOI:10.37236/13960), alongside "Improving SAT Solvers on Orthogonal Latin Square Problems," 2026, arXiv:2605.02132, resolves restricted structural cases but not the unrestricted triple-existence question.
solved_when: An explicit construction of three mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order ten is given, or a proof that no such triple exists.
why: It would advance exact small-design existence and constraint-solving methods.
key_works: Myrvold, 1999, “Negative results for orthogonal triples of Latin squares of order 10”; Bright, Keita, and Stevens, 2026, “Myrvold’s results on orthogonal triples of 10×10 Latin squares: A SAT investigation,” DOI:10.37236/13960; “Improving SAT Solvers on Orthogonal Latin Square Problems,” 2026, arXiv:2605.02132.

title: SIC measurements in every complex dimension
subfield: Optimal transport, topology, and geometric statistics
open: Does every complex Hilbert space of dimension \(d\) contain \(d^2\) equiangular unit vectors? Equivalently, prove or disprove that each complex dimension \(d\) admits a symmetric informationally complete (SIC) quantum measurement.
status: Formulated in the late 1990s (Zauner, 1999, doctoral thesis; Zauner, 2011, “Quantum designs: Foundations of a non-commutative design theory”); many constructions and numerical solutions exist, but an unconditional all-dimensions theorem remains open in the 2026 problem collection (Bandeira et al., 2026, “Randomstrasse 101: Open Problems of 2025,” arXiv:2603.29571).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that a SIC-POVM exists in every complex dimension \(d\), with no dimension excluded.
why: It would settle the existence of highly symmetric measurement designs for quantum-state estimation.
key_works: Zauner, 1999, doctoral thesis; Zauner, 2011, “Quantum designs: Foundations of a non-commutative design theory”; Bandeira et al., 2026, “Randomstrasse 101: Open Problems of 2025,” arXiv:2603.29571.

title: Tenfold cheaper physical reliability qualification
open: Can the cost of physical reliability qualification be cut by at least an order of magnitude without weakening the evidence it provides? Formally, can simulation and accelerated testing — with their development and calibration costs fully accounted — replace all but a tenth of physical test expenditure while still matching preregistered reliability bounds and out-of-condition validation performance?
status: This is a proposed moonshot with no results yet; the accounting requirement is that claimed savings must include simulator development, calibration specimens, and the cost of failed qualification attempts. Related threads include Hong, Zhang, and Meeker, 2018, "Big Data and Reliability Applications: The Complexity Dimension" and Cranmer et al., 2020, "The frontier of simulation-based inference."
solved_when: A qualification methodology achieves at least a 10× reduction in physical test expenditure, matches preregistered reliability bounds, and holds up in out-of-condition validation, with the savings computation including simulator development, calibration specimens, and the cost of failed qualification attempts.
why: It would accelerate product development without weakening reliability evidence, making rigorous qualification economically viable for far more products.
key_works: Hong, Zhang, and Meeker, 2018, “Big Data and Reliability Applications: The Complexity Dimension”; Cranmer et al., 2020, “The frontier of simulation-based inference.”

title: Log-free resilient cores under covariance bounds
open: Does \(O(d/\epsilon)\) samples from any mean-zero distribution whose covariance is bounded by the identity contain a \((1-\epsilon)\)-fraction subset whose empirical second moment is bounded by a universal constant, with constant high probability?
status: Explicitly listed in a 2025 robust-statistics open-problem lecture (University of Washington CSE 599K, 2025, "Lecture 18: Some open problems in robust statistics (and friends)," December 1); the known comparison bound carries an additional logarithmic dimension factor. Related areas include dimension-free matrix concentration in probability and spectral sparsification in combinatorics.
solved_when: An answer — affirmative or negative — to whether \(O(d/\epsilon)\) samples always suffice for such a \((1-\epsilon)\)-fraction subset with universally bounded empirical second moment at constant high probability; in particular, removing or refuting the logarithmic dimension factor present in the known comparison bound.
why: It would sharpen the sample foundations of robust estimation, pinning down the minimal sample size for resilient cores under covariance bounds.
key_works: University of Washington CSE 599K, 2025, “Lecture 18: Some open problems in robust statistics (and friends),” December 1.
